claim: PAK1 inhibitors markedly improve social and cognitive function in several animal models of brain disorders, including autism.
source: PAK1 inhibitors are known to markedly improve social and cognitive function in several animal models of brain disorders, including autism, but the underlying mechanisms remain elusive.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge, supported by citations in the introduction (Dolan et al., 2013; Hayashi et al., 2007; Molosh et al., 2014).

claim: Disruption of PAK1 in mice suppresses inhibitory neurotransmission through an increase in tonic, but not phasic, secretion of endocannabinoids.
source: We show here that disruption of PAK1 in mice suppresses inhibitory neurotransmission through an increase in tonic, but not phasic, secretion of endocannabinoids (eCB).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1-3, 6-8, including measurements of IPSCs, endocannabinoid levels, and pharmacological manipulations.

claim: Levels of anandamide (AEA), but not 2-arachidonoylglycerol (2-AG), are elevated following PAK1 disruption.
source: Consistently, we found elevated levels of anandamide (AEA), but not 2-arachidonoylglycerol (2-AG) following PAK1 disruption.
evidence: This is supported by direct biochemical measurements shown in Figure 7a,b demonstrating increased AEA but unchanged 2-AG levels in PAK1 KO mice.

claim: Increased tonic AEA signaling following PAK1 disruption is mediated by reduced cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2).
source: This increased tonic AEA signaling is mediated by reduced cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2), and COX-2 inhibitors recapitulate the effect of PAK1 deletion on GABAergic transmission in a CB1 receptor-dependent manner.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 7k and 8a,b showing reduced synaptosomal COX-2 in PAK1 KO mice and that COX-2 inhibitor Nimesulide mimics the effect of PAK1 deletion.

claim: COX-2 inhibitors recapitulate the effect of PAK1 deletion on GABAergic transmission in a CB1 receptor-dependent manner.
source: This increased tonic AEA signaling is mediated by reduced cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2), and COX-2 inhibitors recapitulate the effect of PAK1 deletion on GABAergic transmission in a CB1 receptor-dependent manner.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments in Figure 8a,b showing that COX-2 inhibitor Nimesulide produces similar effects to PAK1 deletion, and these effects are reversed by CB1 receptor antagonist AM251.

claim: Normal brain function is dependent upon a balance of excitation and inhibition (balanced E/I ratio).
source: It is generally accepted that normal brain function is dependent upon a balance of excitation and inhibition (i.e. balanced E/I ratio) and that altered E/I ratios are associated with, and thought to cause, a wide range of neurological and mental disorders, including autism and schizophrenia (Eichler and Meier, 2008; Kehrer et al., 2008; Marín, 2012; Yizhar et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as generally accepted knowledge and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Altered E/I ratios are associated with and thought to cause a wide range of neurological and mental disorders, including autism and schizophrenia.
source: It is generally accepted that normal brain function is dependent upon a balance of excitation and inhibition (i.e. balanced E/I ratio) and that altered E/I ratios are associated with, and thought to cause, a wide range of neurological and mental disorders, including autism and schizophrenia (Eichler and Meier, 2008; Kehrer et al., 2008; Marín, 2012; Yizhar et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: GABA-mediated synaptic inhibition is particularly important to maintain an appropriate E/I ratio.
source: Recent studies indicate that GABA-mediated synaptic inhibition is particularly important to maintain an appropriate E/I ratio and that inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs) mediated by GABA receptors are frequently altered in various brain diseases and their animal models (Braat and Kooy, 2015; Lewis et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs) mediated by GABA receptors are frequently altered in various brain diseases and their animal models.
source: Recent studies indicate that GABA-mediated synaptic inhibition is particularly important to maintain an appropriate E/I ratio and that inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs) mediated by GABA receptors are frequently altered in various brain diseases and their animal models (Braat and Kooy, 2015; Lewis et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: GABA transmission is strongly inhibited by endocannabinoids (eCBs).
source: Although subjected to multiple regulations, GABA transmission is strongly inhibited by endocannabinoids (eCBs), a group of neuromodulatory lipids known to affect a wide range of physiological processes and medical conditions (Katona and Freund, 2012; Morena et al., 2016; Piomelli, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: Endocannabinoids are produced and secreted from postsynaptic neurons and activate presynaptic cannabinoid 1 (CB1) receptors to reduce the release of neurotransmitters, including GABA.
source: In the brain, eCBs are produced and secreted from postsynaptic neurons and activate presynaptic cannabinoid 1 (CB1) receptors to reduce the release of a multitude of neurotransmitters, including GABA (Katona and Freund, 2012; Morena et al., 2016; Piomelli, 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Tonic eCB release regulates basal synaptic transmission.
source: Two types of eCB-mediated suppression of GABA release have been studied: tonic eCB release that regulates basal synaptic transmission, and phasic eCB release, induced by postsynaptic depolarization or receptor-mediated eCB production, which mediates transient decreases in synaptic transmission during short-term plasticity (Katona and Freund, 2012; Morena et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Phasic eCB release, induced by postsynaptic depolarization or receptor-mediated eCB production, mediates transient decreases in synaptic transmission during short-term plasticity.
source: Two types of eCB-mediated suppression of GABA release have been studied: tonic eCB release that regulates basal synaptic transmission, and phasic eCB release, induced by postsynaptic depolarization or receptor-mediated eCB production, which mediates transient decreases in synaptic transmission during short-term plasticity (Katona and Freund, 2012; Morena et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Cellular signaling mechanisms that regulate eCB signaling, particularly tonic eCB signaling, remain poorly understood.
source: Although the metabolic process of the eCBs and the enzymes involved in their regulation have been a focus of extensive research (Katona and Freund, 2012; Morena et al., 2016; Piomelli, 2003), cellular signaling mechanisms that regulate eCB signaling, particularly tonic eCB signaling, remain poorly understood.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge despite extensive research on eCB metabolism.

claim: PAKs are activated by multiple synaptic proteins including Ras and Rho GTPases.
source: p21-activated kinases (PAKs) are a family of serine/threonine protein kinases that are activated by multiple synaptic proteins including Ras and Rho GTPases.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PAK activation mechanisms.

claim: PAKs are involved in the regulation of gene expression and cellular cytoskeleton.
source: Extensive studies have indicated that PAKs are involved in a number of cellular processes, particularly in the regulation of gene expression and cellular cytoskeleton (Bokoch, 2003; Zhao and Manser, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: Changes in PAKs are associated with various forms of cancers.
source: Accordingly, changes in PAKs are found to be associated with a wide range of physiological and pathological conditions including various forms of cancers and PAK inhibitors are being actively exploited as therapeutic agents to treat these diseases (Kelly and Chernoff, 2012; Kumar et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: PAK inhibitors are being actively exploited as therapeutic agents to treat cancers.
source: Accordingly, changes in PAKs are found to be associated with a wide range of physiological and pathological conditions including various forms of cancers and PAK inhibitors are being actively exploited as therapeutic agents to treat these diseases (Kelly and Chernoff, 2012; Kumar et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: PAKs are linked to neurological and mental disorders including autism, intellectual disability, Huntingtin's diseases and Alzheimer's diseases.
source: Recent human studies have also revealed that PAKs are linked to a number of devastating neurological and mental disorders including autism, intellectual disability, Huntingtin's diseases and Alzheimer's diseases (Gilman et al., 2011; Ma et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to human studies.

claim: PAK1 is the predominant member of the PAK family expressed in the brain.
source: Animal studies have indeed shown that PAKs, particularly PAK1, the predominant member of the PAK family expressed in the brain, are involved in the regulation of excitatory synaptic function, including spine structure, synaptic plasticity and memory formation (Asrar et al., 2009; Hayashi et al., 2004; Huang et al., 2011; Meng et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PAK1 is involved in the regulation of excitatory synaptic function, including spine structure, synaptic plasticity and memory formation.
source: Animal studies have indeed shown that PAKs, particularly PAK1, the predominant member of the PAK family expressed in the brain, are involved in the regulation of excitatory synaptic function, including spine structure, synaptic plasticity and memory formation (Asrar et al., 2009; Hayashi et al., 2004; Huang et al., 2011; Meng et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to animal studies.

claim: Inhibition of PAK1, either genetically or pharmacologically, can ameliorate the cognitive and social deficits in several animal models of neurodevelopmental disorders, particularly autism.
source: Most remarkably, more recent studies demonstrate that inhibition of PAK1, either genetically or pharmacologically, can ameliorate the cognitive and social deficits in several animal models of neurodevelopmental disorders, particularly autism, including genetic models targeting fragile X syndrome and neurofibromatosis (Dolan et al., 2013; Hayashi et al., 2007; Molosh et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: The mechanism by which PAK1 exerts diverse therapeutic effects remains elusive.
source: However, the mechanism by which PAK1 exerts such diverse therapeutic effects remains elusive.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current understanding.

claim: Animal models of neurodevelopmental disorders exhibit pronounced alterations in eCB signaling.
source: Quite interestingly, many of these same animal models of neurodevelopmental disorders also exhibit pronounced alterations in eCB signaling (Földy et al., 2013; Jung et al., 2012), and several reports have now suggested that, like PAK1, targeting eCB signaling may provide benefit in these conditions (Busquets-Garcia et al., 2013; Qin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: Targeting eCB signaling may provide benefit in neurodevelopmental disorders.
source: Quite interestingly, many of these same animal models of neurodevelopmental disorders also exhibit pronounced alterations in eCB signaling (Földy et al., 2013; Jung et al., 2012), and several reports have now suggested that, like PAK1, targeting eCB signaling may provide benefit in these conditions (Busquets-Garcia et al., 2013; Qin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: Animal models of neurodevelopmental disorders share a common deficit in E/I balance.
source: As these animal models share a common deficit in E/I balance, which appear to involve critical roles of both PAK1 and eCB signaling, we have hypothesized that PAK1 might be a critical player in the regulation of E/I homeostasis through an interaction with eCB signaling.
evidence: This is stated as a rationale for the hypothesis, based on established knowledge.

claim: PAK1 restricts tonic eCB signaling in the hippocampus through the regulation of synaptosomal cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) expression.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, our data indicate that PAK1 restricts tonic eCB signaling in the hippocampus through the regulation of synaptosomal cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) expression, a non-canonical but relevant pathway in the metabolism of eCB signaling.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figures 7k, 8, and 9 showing reduced synaptosomal COX-2 in PAK1 KO mice and effects of COX-2 inhibition.

claim: The E/I ratio is significantly increased in PAK1 KO compared to WT littermates.
source: As shown in Figure 1c, the E/I ratio was significantly increased in PAK1 KO compared to the WT littermates.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: PAK1 KO mice show no deficits in basal excitatory synaptic strength.
source: Because PAK1 KO mice show no deficits in basal excitatory synaptic strength (Asrar et al., 2009), the increased E/I ratio in the KO mice is likely due to impaired inhibitory transmission.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The amplitude of eIPSC is significantly smaller in PAK1 KO compared to WT control over a wide range of stimulus intensities.
source: To test this possibility directly, we performed input/output experiments of eIPSC and as shown in Figure 1d, the amplitude of eIPSC was significantly smaller in the KO compared to the WT control over a wide range of stimulus intensities.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Bath application of IPA3 (10 μM) caused a rapid and significant decrease in the amplitude of eIPSC in WT, but not in PAK1 KO neurons.
source: As shown in Figure 1e, bath application of IPA3 caused a rapid and significant decrease in the amplitude of eIPSC in WT, but not in PAK1 KO neurons.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Inclusion of PAK1 inhibitory peptide in postsynaptic neurons (20 μg/ml) significantly decreased the amplitude of eIPSC in WT, but not in PAK1 KO neurons.
source: As shown in Figure 1f, inclusion of this peptide in the postsynaptic neurons (20 μg/ml) also significantly decreased the amplitude of eIPSC in WT, but not in PAK1 KO neurons.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: The fast acting nature of PAK1 inhibitors indicates that the effect of PAK1 on eIPSC is not likely due to a developmental effect but rather direct involvement of PAK1 at the synapse.
source: The fast acting nature of these inhibitors (within minutes) indicate that the effect of PAK1 on eIPSC is not likely due to a developmental effect but rather direct involvement of PAK1 at the synapse.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rapid time course of the effects observed in Figures 1e and 1f.

claim: PAK1 disruption specifically in postsynaptic CA1 neurons is sufficient to cause impaired inhibitory synaptic transmission.
source: These results also indicate that PAK1 disruption specifically in the postsynaptic CA1 neurons is sufficient to cause impaired inhibitory synaptic transmission.
evidence: This is inferred from the experiments using postsynaptic infusion of PAK1 inhibitors shown in Figures 1f and 3.

claim: The frequency of sIPSC is significantly reduced in PAK1 KO compared to WT neurons.
source: As shown in Figure 2a–f, the frequency of sIPSC (Figure 2c) and mIPSC (Figure 2f) was significantly reduced in PAK1 KO compared to WT neurons.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The frequency of mIPSC is significantly reduced in PAK1 KO compared to WT neurons.
source: As shown in Figure 2a–f, the frequency of sIPSC (Figure 2c) and mIPSC (Figure 2f) was significantly reduced in PAK1 KO compared to WT neurons.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: The amplitude of sIPSC is not altered in PAK1 KO mice.
source: The amplitude of sIPSC (Figure 2b) and mIPSC (Figure 2e) were not altered in the KO mice.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The amplitude of mIPSC is not altered in PAK1 KO mice.
source: The amplitude of sIPSC (Figure 2b) and mIPSC (Figure 2e) were not altered in the KO mice.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Neither the frequency nor the amplitude of spontaneous or miniature excitatory synaptic currents (sEPSC or mEPSC) is altered in PAK1 KO mice.
source: Consistent with previous results (Asrar et al., 2009), neither the frequency nor the amplitude of spontaneous or miniature excitatory synaptic currents (sEPSC or mEPSC) was altered in PAK1 KO mice (Figure 2g–i).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2g-i and consistent with previous citations.

claim: No significant changes in sIPSC or mIPSC parameters are found in ROCK2 KO mice.
source: To test whether these changes were specific to PAK1 KO mice, we analyzed KO mice lacking ROCK2 (Zhou et al., 2009), a closely related kinase also activated by the Rho family small GTPases, but found no significant changes in any of these parameters in these mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The release property at the inhibitory synapse is selectively impaired in PAK1 KO neurons.
source: These results suggest that the release property at the inhibitory synapse is selectively impaired in PAK1 KO neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the reduced frequency but normal amplitude of sIPSC and mIPSC in PAK1 KO mice.

claim: Synaptic depression induced by 3 min of 5 Hz stimulations is significantly slower in PAK1 KO mice compared to WT littermates.
source: As shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2, synaptic depression induced by 3 min of 5 Hz stimulations was significantly slower in PAK1 KO mice compared to the WT littermates.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: PAK1 regulates inhibitory synaptic transmission likely through a presynaptic mechanism.
source: These results indicate that PAK1 regulates inhibitory synaptic transmission likely through a presynaptic mechanism.
evidence: This is inferred from the reduced frequency but normal amplitude of IPSCs and altered synaptic depression.

claim: Inclusion of IPA3 caused a significant decrease in the frequency, but not the amplitude of sIPSC in WT neurons.
source: As shown in Figure 3a–c, inclusion of IPA3 caused a significant decrease in the frequency (Figure 3c), but not the amplitude (Figure 3b) of sIPSC in WT neurons.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3a-c.

claim: IPA3 significantly reduced the frequency, but not the amplitude of mIPSC in WT neurons.
source: IPA3 also significantly reduced the frequency (Figure 3d,f), but not the amplitude (Figure 3d,e) of mIPSC in WT neurons.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3d-f.

claim: IPA3 had no effect on the frequency of sIPSC and mIPSC in PAK1 KO mice.
source: Importantly, IPA3 had no effect on the frequency of sIPSC and mIPSC in PAK1 KO mice (Figure 3a,c,d,f), again confirming that the effect of IPA3 is mediated by PAK1.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3a,c,d,f.

claim: Neither the frequency nor the amplitude of sEPSC or mEPSC is affected by IPA3.
source: Neither the frequency nor the amplitude of sEPSC or mEPSC was affected by IPA3 (Figure 3g–i).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3g-i.

claim: Disruption of postsynaptic PAK1 is sufficient to reduce presynaptic release of inhibitory neurotransmitters.
source: The rapid and selective effect of IPA3 on the frequency of sIPSC and mIPSC again suggests that disruption of postsynaptic PAK1 is sufficient to reduce presynaptic release of inhibitory neurotransmitters.
evidence: This is inferred from the rapid effects of postsynaptic IPA3 infusion on IPSC frequency shown in Figure 3.

claim: The number of GABAergic neurons is similar in PAK1 KO and WT control mice.
source: To address this possibility, we first examined the number of GABA-positive neurons and inhibitory synapses, and the level of GABA receptor associated proteins, but found no significant differences between WT and PAK1 KO mice (Figure 4a–e; also see Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4a,b.

claim: The number of inhibitory synapses is similar in PAK1 KO and WT control mice.
source: To address this possibility, we first examined the number of GABA-positive neurons and inhibitory synapses, and the level of GABA receptor associated proteins, but found no significant differences between WT and PAK1 KO mice (Figure 4a–e; also see Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4c,d.

claim: The level of GABA receptor associated proteins is similar in PAK1 KO and WT control mice.
source: To address this possibility, we first examined the number of GABA-positive neurons and inhibitory synapses, and the level of GABA receptor associated proteins, but found no significant differences between WT and PAK1 KO mice (Figure 4a–e; also see Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: No differences in GABA receptor function are found between WT and PAK1 KO neurons.
source: To determine if GABA receptors were functionally equivalent, we recorded IPSCs evoked by a brief puff of GABA (1 mM, 100 ms) in a co-culture system where WT and PAK1 KO neurons were grown on the same coverlips in order to minimize the differences in culturing conditions between genotypes (see Materials and methods), but again found no differences between WT and PAK1 KO neurons (Figure 4f,g).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4f,g.

claim: Cytochalasin D has no effect on sIPSCs.
source: As shown in Figure 5a–f, no effect on sIPSCs was observed for either inhibitor.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5a-c.

claim: NSC23766 has no effect on sIPSCs.
source: As shown in Figure 5a–f, no effect on sIPSCs was observed for either inhibitor.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5d-f.

claim: Cytochalasin D and NSC23766 have profound effects on excitatory synaptic function, including basal synaptic transmission.
source: It is important to note that consistent with previous results (Meng et al., 2002; Zhou et al., 2011), these two inhibitors (at the same concentrations used here) had profound effects on excitatory synaptic function, including basal synaptic transmission (Figure 5g–i) and metabotropic glutamate receptor (mGluR)-dependent long-term depression induced by 50 μM DHPG (Figure 5j,k).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5g-k and consistent with previous citations.

claim: Postsynaptic PAK1 regulates inhibitory synaptic transmission likely through a retrograde mechanism to modulate GABA release.
source: Taken together, we concluded that postsynaptic PAK1 regulates inhibitory synaptic transmission likely through a retrograde mechanism to modulate GABA release.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of postsynaptic changes in GABA receptors or cytoskeleton effects, combined with the presynaptic phenotype.

claim: Bath application of AM251 (5 μM) increased eIPSCs to approximately 150% of the baseline response in WT.
source: In WT, bath application of AM251 (5 μM) increased eIPSCs to approximately 150% of the baseline response (Figure 6a), reflecting disinhibition of GABA release by blocking tonically active CB1 receptors (Neu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: In PAK1 KO mice, AM251 enhanced eIPSC amplitudes to 250% of the baseline response.
source: Remarkably, in PAK1 KO mice, AM251 enhanced eIPSC amplitudes to 250% of the baseline response (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Acute inhibition of postsynaptic PAK1 by IPA3 (10 μM) prior to AM251 application produced similar results as shown in PAK1 KO mice.
source: Acute inhibition of postsynaptic PAK1 by IPA3 (10 μM) or by the PAK1 inhibitory peptide (20 μg/ml) prior to the AM251 application produced similar results as shown in PAK1 KO mice (Figure 6b,c).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Acute inhibition of postsynaptic PAK1 by the PAK1 inhibitory peptide (20 μg/ml) prior to AM251 application produced similar results as shown in PAK1 KO mice.
source: Acute inhibition of postsynaptic PAK1 by IPA3 (10 μM) or by the PAK1 inhibitory peptide (20 μg/ml) prior to the AM251 application produced similar results as shown in PAK1 KO mice (Figure 6b,c).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: Tonic eCB signaling is restricted by PAK1 and disruption of PAK1 causes a robust increase in tonic eCB effect.
source: These findings indicate that tonic eCB signaling is restricted by PAK1 and that disruption of PAK1 causes a robust increase in tonic eCB effect.
evidence: This is inferred from the enhanced effect of AM251 in PAK1 KO mice shown in Figure 6a-c.

claim: No differences in CB1 receptor protein levels are found in either total brain lysates or synaptosomal fractions between WT and PAK1 KO mice.
source: To further investigate whether the enhanced eCB signaling in the KO mice is due to changes in CB receptors and/or their downstream signaling processes in the presynaptic terminal, we examined the protein level of CB1 receptors, but found no differences in either total brain lysates (Figure 6d) or synaptosomal fractions (Figure 6e).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6d,e.

claim: Bath application of the CB1 receptor agonist WIN (5 μM) depressed synaptic responses to the same degree in both WT and PAK1 KO mice.
source: In addition, bath application of the CB1 receptor agonist WIN (5 μM), designed to maximally activate the receptor, depressed synaptic responses to the same degree in both WT and PAK1 KO mice (Figure 6f), suggesting that CB1 receptors and their downstream events are intact in the KO mice.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6f.

claim: CB1 receptors and their downstream events are intact in PAK1 KO mice.
source: In addition, bath application of the CB1 receptor agonist WIN (5 μM), designed to maximally activate the receptor, depressed synaptic responses to the same degree in both WT and PAK1 KO mice (Figure 6f), suggesting that CB1 receptors and their downstream events are intact in the KO mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the equivalent response to WIN in WT and PAK1 KO mice shown in Figure 6f.

claim: Tissue levels of AEA are significantly elevated in PAK1 KO mice.
source: Interestingly, tissue levels of AEA (Figure 7a), but not 2-AG (Figure 7b), were significantly elevated in PAK1 KO mice.
evidence: This is supported by biochemical measurements shown in Figure 7a.

claim: Tissue levels of 2-AG are not altered in PAK1 KO mice.
source: Interestingly, tissue levels of AEA (Figure 7a), but not 2-AG (Figure 7b), were significantly elevated in PAK1 KO mice.
evidence: This is supported by biochemical measurements shown in Figure 7b.

claim: AEA mediates tonic actions of the eCB system.
source: These data are consistent with the belief that AEA mediates tonic actions of the eCB system (Di et al., 2013; Kim and Alger, 2010; Tabatadze et al., 2015), whereas 2-AG mediates essentially all forms of phasic eCB signaling in the CNS (Katona and Freund, 2012; Morena et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: 2-AG mediates essentially all forms of phasic eCB signaling in the CNS.
source: These data are consistent with the belief that AEA mediates tonic actions of the eCB system (Di et al., 2013; Kim and Alger, 2010; Tabatadze et al., 2015), whereas 2-AG mediates essentially all forms of phasic eCB signaling in the CNS (Katona and Freund, 2012; Morena et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: AEA mediates tonic inhibition of GABA release within the hippocampus.
source: More so, as AEA mediates tonic inhibition of GABA release within the hippocampus (Di et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2015; Tabatadze et al., 2015), these data indicate that PAK1 disruption results in an increase in AEA production and a consequential reduction in tonic GABA release.
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: PAK1 disruption results in an increase in AEA production and a consequential reduction in tonic GABA release.
source: More so, as AEA mediates tonic inhibition of GABA release within the hippocampus (Di et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2015; Tabatadze et al., 2015), these data indicate that PAK1 disruption results in an increase in AEA production and a consequential reduction in tonic GABA release.
evidence: This is inferred from the elevated AEA levels and reduced GABA transmission in PAK1 KO mice.

claim: The amplitude of DSI is significantly reduced in PAK1 KO compared to WT mice.
source: To investigate whether this interaction occurs in PAK1 KO mice, we analyzed phasic suppression of inhibition induced by postsynaptic depolarization (DSI) and found that the amplitude of DSI was significantly reduced in the KO compared to WT mice (Figure 7c), supporting the idea that elevated AEA competes with 2-AG, resulting in reduced phasic 2-AG signaling.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 7c.

claim: Elevated AEA competes with 2-AG, resulting in reduced phasic 2-AG signaling.
source: To investigate whether this interaction occurs in PAK1 KO mice, we analyzed phasic suppression of inhibition induced by postsynaptic depolarization (DSI) and found that the amplitude of DSI was significantly reduced in the KO compared to WT mice (Figure 7c), supporting the idea that elevated AEA competes with 2-AG, resulting in reduced phasic 2-AG signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the reduced DSI in PAK1 KO mice and supported by citation to Lee et al., 2015.

claim: Disruption of PAK1 selectively augments tonic AEA signaling to dampen constitutive synaptic GABA transmission.
source: Together, these data create a compelling argument that disruption of PAK1 selectively augments tonic AEA signaling to dampen constitutive synaptic GABA transmission.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data showing elevated AEA, reduced GABA transmission, and reduced DSI in PAK1 KO mice.

claim: Enzymes involved in the generation and metabolism of 2-AG, including MGL and DGL, are not altered in PAK1 KO mice.
source: Consistent with the fact that there were no changes in 2-AG, the enzymes involved in the generation and metabolism of 2-AG, including monoacylglycerol lipase (MGL) and diacylglycerol lipase (DGL), were not altered in PAK1 KO mice (Figure 7d–g).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7d-g.

claim: Both total and synaptosomal protein levels of FAAH are not altered in PAK1 KO mice.
source: Surprisingly, however, both total and synaptosomal protein levels of the enzyme primarily involved in AEA metabolism, fatty acid amide hydrolase (FAAH), were also not altered in PAK1 KO mice (Figure 7h,i).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7h,i.

claim: Total protein level of COX-2 is not altered in PAK1 KO mice.
source: Notably, we found that although the total protein level of COX-2 was not altered (Figure 7j), its synaptosomal fraction was significantly reduced in the KO brain (Figure 7k, Figure 7—figure supplement 1), suggesting that PAK1 is specifically important for COX-2 expression at the synapse and/or during synaptic activity.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7j.

claim: Synaptosomal COX-2 is significantly reduced in PAK1 KO brain.
source: Notably, we found that although the total protein level of COX-2 was not altered (Figure 7j), its synaptosomal fraction was significantly reduced in the KO brain (Figure 7k, Figure 7—figure supplement 1), suggesting that PAK1 is specifically important for COX-2 expression at the synapse and/or during synaptic activity.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7k and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: PAK1 is specifically important for COX-2 expression at the synapse and/or during synaptic activity.
source: Notably, we found that although the total protein level of COX-2 was not altered (Figure 7j), its synaptosomal fraction was significantly reduced in the KO brain (Figure 7k, Figure 7—figure supplement 1), suggesting that PAK1 is specifically important for COX-2 expression at the synapse and/or during synaptic activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the selective reduction in synaptosomal, but not total, COX-2 in PAK1 KO mice.

claim: The enhanced eCB signaling due to the disruption of PAK1 might be mediated by reduced COX-2 and subsequently elevated AEA.
source: Together these results suggest that the enhanced eCB signaling, due to the disruption of PAK1, might be mediated by reduced COX-2 and subsequently elevated AEA.
evidence: This is inferred from the reduced synaptosomal COX-2 and elevated AEA in PAK1 KO mice.

claim: Application of Nimesulide (30 μM) in WT neurons depressed IPSCs to approximately 45% of the baseline response.
source: As shown in Figure 8a, application of Nimesulide (30 μM) in WT neurons depressed IPSCs to approximately 45% of the baseline response, presumably due to increased eCB production, but this Nimesulide-induced depression was significantly reduced (to 70% of the baseline response) in PAK1 KO neurons, consistent with an already reduced COX-2 level in the KO mice.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 8a.

claim: Nimesulide-induced depression of IPSCs is significantly reduced in PAK1 KO neurons compared to WT.
source: As shown in Figure 8a, application of Nimesulide (30 μM) in WT neurons depressed IPSCs to approximately 45% of the baseline response, presumably due to increased eCB production, but this Nimesulide-induced depression was significantly reduced (to 70% of the baseline response) in PAK1 KO neurons, consistent with an already reduced COX-2 level in the KO mice.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 8a.

claim: Following Nimesulide application, both WT and PAK1 KO neurons showed equally enhanced responses (250% of the baseline response) to AM251.
source: As shown in Figure 8b, both WT and PAK1 KO neurons now showed equally enhanced responses (250% of the baseline response) that were similar to PAK1 KO neurons treated with AM251 alone as shown in Figure 6a.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 8b.

claim: Inhibition of COX-2 in WT neurons recapitulated the effect of PAK1 disruption.
source: Therefore, inhibition of COX-2 in WT neurons recapitulated the effect of PAK1 disruption.
evidence: This is inferred from the data in Figure 8a,b showing that COX-2 inhibition produces similar effects to PAK1 deletion.

claim: Bath application of URB597 (1 μM) depressed eIPSC in WT mice, but this depression was reduced in PAK1 KO mice.
source: Similar to what was seen following COX-2 inhibition, the ability of the FAAH inhibitor URB597 (1 μM) to reduce eIPSC was reduced in PAK1 KO mice relative to WT mice (Figure 8c) and the effect of AM251 (5 μM) on eIPSC was no longer different between the two genotypes after the FAAH treatment (Figure 8d), consistent with the fact that there is already an elevated AEA tone.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 8c.

claim: The effect of AM251 on eIPSC is no longer different between WT and PAK1 KO genotypes after FAAH inhibitor treatment.
source: Similar to what was seen following COX-2 inhibition, the ability of the FAAH inhibitor URB597 (1 μM) to reduce eIPSC was reduced in PAK1 KO mice relative to WT mice (Figure 8c) and the effect of AM251 (5 μM) on eIPSC was no longer different between the two genotypes after the FAAH treatment (Figure 8d), consistent with the fact that there is already an elevated AEA tone.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 8d.

claim: Bath application of JZL184 (5 μM) depressed eIPSC to the same degree in both WT and KO neurons.
source: Importantly, the effect of the MGL inhibitor JZL184 was not altered in PAK1 KO mice; that is, bath application of JZL184 (5 μM) depressed eIPSC to the same degree in both WT and KO neurons (Figure 8e) and had no effects on the degree of disinhibition by AM251 (5 μM) (Figure 8f).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 8e.

claim: JZL184 had no effects on the degree of disinhibition by AM251 in PAK1 KO mice.
source: Importantly, the effect of the MGL inhibitor JZL184 was not altered in PAK1 KO mice; that is, bath application of JZL184 (5 μM) depressed eIPSC to the same degree in both WT and KO neurons (Figure 8e) and had no effects on the degree of disinhibition by AM251 (5 μM) (Figure 8f).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 8f.

claim: The increased inhibition of GABA transmission by eCB signaling in PAK1 KO mice is caused by reduced COX-2 expression and consequential elevation in AEA, but not 2-AG, signaling at GABA synapses in the CA1 region of the hippocampus.
source: Therefore, we conclude that the increased inhibition of GABA transmission by eCB signaling in PAK1 KO mice is caused by reduced COX-2 expression and consequential elevation in AEA, but not 2-AG, signaling at GABA synapses in the CA1 region of the hippocampus.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data from Figures 7 and 8 showing reduced synaptosomal COX-2, elevated AEA, and differential effects of AEA vs 2-AG pathway inhibitors.

claim: In WT neurons, PAK1 is colocalized with both PSD-95 (excitatory synaptic marker) and gephyrin (GABAergic synaptic marker).
source: First, we showed that in WT neurons, PAK1 was colocalized with both PSD-95 (excitatory synaptic marker, Figure 9a) and gephyrin (GABAergic synaptic marker, Figure 9b), suggesting that PAK1 is expressed at both excitatory and inhibitory synapses.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 9a,b.

claim: PAK1 is expressed at both excitatory and inhibitory synapses.
source: First, we showed that in WT neurons, PAK1 was colocalized with both PSD-95 (excitatory synaptic marker, Figure 9a) and gephyrin (GABAergic synaptic marker, Figure 9b), suggesting that PAK1 is expressed at both excitatory and inhibitory synapses.
evidence: This is inferred from the colocalization data shown in Figure 9a,b.

claim: PAK1 is colocalized with COX-2.
source: In addition, we showed that PAK1 was colocalized with COX-2 (Figure 9c).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 9c.

claim: A small portion of COX-2 is colocalized with PSD-95 and this colocalization is not altered in PAK1 KO neurons.
source: Next, we showed that a small portion of COX-2 was colocalized with PSD-95 (Figure 9d) and this colocalization was not altered in PAK1 KO neurons (Figure 9e–h), suggesting that PAK1 disruption does not affect COX-2 localization at the excitatory synapse.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 9d-h.

claim: PAK1 disruption does not affect COX-2 localization at the excitatory synapse.
source: Next, we showed that a small portion of COX-2 was colocalized with PSD-95 (Figure 9d) and this colocalization was not altered in PAK1 KO neurons (Figure 9e–h), suggesting that PAK1 disruption does not affect COX-2 localization at the excitatory synapse.
evidence: This is inferred from the unchanged colocalization of COX-2 with PSD-95 in PAK1 KO neurons shown in Figure 9h.

claim: A much larger portion of COX-2 is colocalized with gephyrin.
source: Finally, we showed that a much larger portion of COX-2 was colocalized with gephyrin (Figure 9i), and importantly, the level of this colocalization was significantly reduced in PAK1 KO compared to WT neurons (Figure 9i–m).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 9i.

claim: The level of COX-2 colocalization with gephyrin is significantly reduced in PAK1 KO compared to WT neurons.
source: Finally, we showed that a much larger portion of COX-2 was colocalized with gephyrin (Figure 9i), and importantly, the level of this colocalization was significantly reduced in PAK1 KO compared to WT neurons (Figure 9i–m).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 9i-m.

claim: Total protein levels of COX-2, PSD-95, and gephyrin are unaltered in PAK1 KO neurons.
source: The total protein levels of COX-2 (Figure 9f,k), PSD-95 (Figure 9g) and gephyrin (Figure 9l) were unaltered in PAK1 KO neurons.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining quantification data shown in Figure 9f,g,k,l.

claim: PAK1 disruption specifically impairs COX-2 localization at GABAergic synapses.
source: These results together suggest that PAK1 disruption specifically impairs COX-2 localization at GBABergic synapses, providing a mechanism for PAK1-COX2 signaling to specifically regulate inhibitory synaptic transmission.
evidence: This is inferred from the selective reduction in COX-2 colocalization with gephyrin but not PSD-95 in PAK1 KO neurons shown in Figure 9.

claim: PAK1-COX2 signaling specifically regulates inhibitory synaptic transmission.
source: These results together suggest that PAK1 disruption specifically impairs COX-2 localization at GBABergic synapses, providing a mechanism for PAK1-COX2 signaling to specifically regulate inhibitory synaptic transmission.
evidence: This is inferred from the selective effect of PAK1 on COX-2 at GABAergic synapses and the selective effect on inhibitory transmission.

claim: These data represent the first demonstration of a physiological substrate (PAK1) which can mobilize COX-2 to the synaptic compartment to modulate eCB signaling in real time.
source: While several reports have identified COX-2 as a regulator of eCB signaling, these data represent the first demonstration of a physiological substrate (PAK1 in this case), which can mobilize COX-2 to the synaptic compartment to modulate eCB signaling in real time.
evidence: This is stated as a novel contribution of the current study.

claim: These data provide some of the first data regarding intracellular signaling mechanisms that can regulate tonic AEA signaling.
source: In addition, these data provide some of the first data regarding intracellular signaling mechanisms that can regulate tonic AEA signaling and, importantly, could potentially have significant implications for a wide range of pathologies that involve dysregulation of this cascade.
evidence: This is stated as a novel contribution of the current study.

claim: PAK1 is known to be important in the regulation of spine properties such as spine actin and morphology, but its effect on excitatory synaptic transmission is minimal.
source: Although PAK1 is known to be important in the regulation of spine properties such as spine actin and morphology, its effect on excitatory synaptic transmission is minimal (Asrar et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Basal excitatory synaptic transmission is not altered in PAK1 KO mice, possibly due to the existence of other functionally redundant PAKs (e.g. PAK2 and PAK3).
source: In fact, basal excitatory synaptic transmission is not altered in PAK1 KO mice, possibly due to the existence of other functionally redundant PAKs (e.g. PAK2 and PAK3) (Bokoch, 2003; Huang et al., 2011; Kelly and Chernoff, 2012; Meng et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated as an explanation supported by citations.

claim: Disruptions of PAK1, either by genetic deletion or pharmacological blockade, dramatically reduces GABAergic transmission.
source: In contrast, disruptions of PAK1, either by genetic deletion or pharmacological blockade, dramatically reduces GABAergic transmission, indicating that the primary role of PAK1 is to facilitate inhibitory but not excitatory synaptic function.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from Figures 1-3.

claim: The primary role of PAK1 is to facilitate inhibitory but not excitatory synaptic function.
source: In contrast, disruptions of PAK1, either by genetic deletion or pharmacological blockade, dramatically reduces GABAergic transmission, indicating that the primary role of PAK1 is to facilitate inhibitory but not excitatory synaptic function.
evidence: This is inferred from the selective effect of PAK1 disruption on inhibitory transmission.

claim: Expression of a dominant negative form of PAK1 affects excitatory synaptic morphology.
source: This selective effect of PAK1 disruption is rather surprising because it has been shown previously that expression of a dominant negative form (i.e. the autoinhibitory domain) of PAK1 affects the excitatory synaptic morphology (Hayashi et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Expression of mutant PAK1 may affect other members of the PAK family, including PAK3.
source: One possible explanation is that the expression of this mutant PAK1 may affect other members of the PAK family, including PAK3, which is also highly expressed in the brain (Meng et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated as a possible explanation supported by citation.

claim: Double KO mice lacking both PAK1 and PAK3 display severe deficits in spines and the actin cytoskeleton.
source: Indeed, the double KO mice lacking both PAK1 and PAK3 display severe deficits in spines and the actin cytoskeleton (Huang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: While PAK1 and PAK3 are functionally redundant at the excitatory synapses, PAK1 is a unique regulator at the inhibitory synapses, which may not be readily replaced by other members of the PAK family.
source: These results together suggest that while PAK1 and PAK3 are functionally redundant at the excitatory synapses, PAK1 is a unique regulator at the inhibitory synapses, which may not be readily replaced by other members of the PAK family.
evidence: This is inferred from the selective effect of PAK1 deletion on inhibitory synapses and the redundancy at excitatory synapses.

claim: The ability of PAK1 inhibitors to ameliorate deficits in models of fragile X syndrome and neurofibromatosis may be mediated by its effect on GABA function.
source: Therefore, the ability of the PAK1 inhibitors in ameliorating the deficits associated with models of fragile X syndrome and neurofibromatosis (Dolan et al., 2013; Hayashi et al., 2007; Molosh et al., 2014) may be mediated by its effect on the GABA function.
evidence: This is speculated based on the findings and supported by citations.

claim: Inhibitory synaptic transmission is commonly altered in brain disorders including fragile X syndrome and neurofibromatosis.
source: Consistent with this notion, inhibitory synaptic transmission is commonly altered in these brain disorders (Cui et al., 2008; Olmos-Serrano et al., 2010; Radhu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: The reduction in IPSC frequency in PAK1 KO mice is not caused by changes in the number of inhibitory neurons or synapses.
source: The reduction in the frequency is not caused by changes in the number of inhibitory neurons or synapses because none of these parameters are altered in the KO mice.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4a-d showing no changes in neuron or synapse numbers.

claim: The lack of changes in synapse number is consistent with the observations that the frequency reduction can be rapidly induced (within mins) by infusion of PAK1 inhibitors.
source: The lack of changes in synapse number is also consistent with the observations that the frequency reduction can be rapidly induced (within mins) by infusion of the PAK1 inhibitors, a perturbation that is not likely to cause any changes in the number of neurons or synapses.
evidence: This is inferred from the rapid time course of inhibitor effects shown in Figures 1e,f and 3.

claim: The frequency reduction induced by PAK1 inhibition is independent of postsynaptic GABA receptors or the actin cytoskeleton.
source: Our data also indicate that although the frequency reduction is induced by postsynaptic inhibition of PAK1, it is independent of postsynaptic GABA receptors or the actin cytoskeleton.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 4 and 5 showing no changes in GABA receptors and no effects of actin/Rac1 inhibitors on IPSCs.

claim: Postsynaptic PAK1 affects GABA transmission through a retrograde messenger to modulate neurotransmitter release.
source: Therefore, postsynaptic PAK1 affects GABA transmission through a retrograde messenger to modulate neurotransmitter release.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of postsynaptic changes and the presynaptic phenotype.

claim: Loss of PAK1 results in increased tonic eCB signaling and therefore a greater inhibition of GABA release.
source: The simplest interpretation of this result is that loss of PAK1 results in increased tonic eCB signaling and therefore a greater inhibition of GABA release.
evidence: This is inferred from the enhanced effect of AM251 in PAK1 KO mice shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Blocking eCB inhibition causes a greater potentiation of GABA release and eIPSC in the absence of PAK1.
source: Thus, blocking eCB inhibition causes a greater potentiation of GABA release and eIPSC in the absence of PAK1.
evidence: This is inferred from the enhanced effect of AM251 in PAK1 KO mice shown in Figure 6a.

claim: eCB signaling can be enhanced by an increase in the signaling pool of eCB molecules and/or altered signaling processes triggered by activation of CB1 receptors.
source: There are at least two possibilities by which the eCB signaling can be enhanced: an increase in the signaling pool of eCB molecules and/or altered signaling processes triggered by activation of the CB1 receptors.
evidence: This is stated as logical possibilities for the mechanism.

claim: eCB secretion is elevated in the absence of PAK1.
source: Because neither the expression level of CB1 receptors nor the effect of a CB1 receptor agonist are enhanced, a straightforward interpretation would be that eCB secretion is elevated in the absence of PAK1.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of changes in CB1 receptors or their activation shown in Figure 6d-f.

claim: The selective increase in AEA is consistent with the fact that tonic, but not phasic, eCB signaling is enhanced by disruption of PAK1.
source: As such, the selective increase in AEA is consistent with the fact that tonic, but not phasic, eCB signaling is enhanced by disruption of PAK1.
evidence: This is inferred from the elevated AEA but not 2-AG in PAK1 KO mice shown in Figure 7a,b.

claim: Elevations in AEA signaling reduce the ability of 2-AG signaling to modulate GABAergic transmission in the hippocampus.
source: In fact, a recent report has suggested that elevations in AEA signaling reduce the ability of 2-AG signaling to modulate GABAergic transmission in the hippocampus (Lee et al., 2015), and again consistent with this finding, our data demonstrate that DSI, a measure of activity-dependent, phasic eCB signaling that is mediated by 2-AG, is reduced in PAK1 KO mice.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2015.

claim: DSI is a measure of activity-dependent, phasic eCB signaling that is mediated by 2-AG.
source: In fact, a recent report has suggested that elevations in AEA signaling reduce the ability of 2-AG signaling to modulate GABAergic transmission in the hippocampus (Lee et al., 2015), and again consistent with this finding, our data demonstrate that DSI, a measure of activity-dependent, phasic eCB signaling that is mediated by 2-AG, is reduced in PAK1 KO mice.
evidence: This is established knowledge.

claim: PAK1 KO mice exhibit no alteration to the synaptic response of a 2-AG hydrolysis inhibitor, but do demonstrate reduced responses to an AEA-hydrolysis inhibitor.
source: Finally, PAK1 KO mice exhibit no alteration to the synaptic response of a 2-AG hydrolysis inhibitor, but do demonstrate reduced responses to a AEA-hydrolysis inhibitor, which is to be expected if PAK1 deletion selectively increases AEA, and not 2-AG, signaling.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 8c-f showing differential effects of FAAH vs MGL inhibitors.

claim: PAK1 normally restricts tonic AEA level to enhance GABA release and maintains sufficient inhibitory transmission.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that PAK1 normally restricts tonic AEA level to enhance GABA release and maintains sufficient inhibitory transmission.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the data showing PAK1's role in restricting AEA and maintaining GABA transmission.

claim: If AEA synthesis were increased by PAK1 deletion, then the effects of an AEA hydrolysis inhibitor would be expected to be amplified, not impaired.
source: The disruption of PAK1 could increase AEA signaling through a variety of mechanisms, although if AEA synthesis were increased by PAK1 deletion, then the effects of an AEA hydrolysis inhibitor would be expected to be amplified, not impaired, because the inhibitor would lock all of the excess AEA within the synapse.
evidence: This is stated as a logical argument for why increased synthesis is unlikely.

claim: If PAK1 disruption reduced AEA hydrolysis, one would expect an occlusion to the addition of an AEA-hydrolysis inhibitor.
source: If PAK1 disruption reduced AEA hydrolysis, however, one would expect an occlusion to the addition of an AEA-hydrolysis inhibitor.
evidence: This is stated as a logical argument for why reduced hydrolysis is likely.

claim: FAAH is the primary enzyme responsible for AEA hydrolysis.
source: FAAH is the primary enzyme responsible for AEA hydrolysis, however our biochemical analysis did not reveal any difference between total or synaptic expression of FAAH protein in PAK1 KO mice.
evidence: This is established knowledge.

claim: Aside from the canonical metabolism of AEA by FAAH, COX-2 represents an additional mechanism of AEA clearance.
source: A growing body of work has identified that aside from the canonical metabolism of AEA by FAAH, COX-2 represents an additional mechanism of AEA clearance (Glaser and Kaczocha, 2010; Hermanson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: The impact of COX-2 inhibition on AEA levels is roughly comparable to the increase documented in PAK1 KO mice.
source: Notably, the impact of COX-2 inhibition on AEA levels (Hermanson et al., 2013) is roughly comparable to the increase we documented herein in PAK1 KO mice.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison supported by citation.

claim: Only synaptic, but not total COX-2 is affected in PAK1 KO mice, implying that PAK1 is particularly important for COX-2 regulation at the synapse.
source: It is important to emphasize that only synaptic, but not total COX-2 is affected in PAK1 KO mice, implying that PAK1 is particularly important for COX-2 regulation at the synapse.
evidence: This is inferred from the selective reduction in synaptosomal COX-2 shown in Figure 7k.

claim: COX-2 is expressed at both excitatory and inhibitory synapses, but the effect of PAK1 deletion on COX-2 appears to be specific to inhibitory synapses.
source: Furthermore, although COX-2 is expressed at both excitatory and inhibitory synapses, the effect of PAK1 deletion on COX-2 appears to be specific to inhibitory synapses, which may contribute to the specific effect of PAK1-COX-2 signaling on inhibitory synaptic transmission.
evidence: This is inferred from the immunostaining data in Figure 9 showing selective reduction in COX-2 at GABAergic synapses.

claim: The mechanism by which PAK1 regulates COX-2 localization is unknown, but it is possible that local regulation of COX-2, both at the level of protein synthesis and/or trafficking, could be targeted by PAK1.
source: The mechanism by which PAK1 regulates COX-2 localization is unknown, but it is possible that local regulation of COX-2, both at the level of protein synthesis and/or trafficking, could be targeted by PAK1.
evidence: This is stated as speculation about possible mechanisms.

claim: PAK1 deletion has been shown to normalize synaptic and behavioral deficits in the Neurofibromatosis model of autism.
source: For example, PAK1 deletion has been shown to normalize synaptic and behavioral deficits in the Neurofibromatosis model of autism (Molosh et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Deletion of PAK1 resulted in a reduction of mIPSC in the amygdala that was associated with an improvement in social behaviors.
source: Specifically, deletion of PAK1 resulted in a reduction of mIPSC in the amygdala (similar to what was found within the hippocampus within the current study) that was associated with an improvement in social behaviors (Molosh et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Elevating AEA signaling within the amygdala has been shown to dampen GABA release in the amygdala and improve social interaction and increase social behavior.
source: In line with this, elevating AEA signaling within the amygdala (which has been shown to dampen GABA release in the amygdala [Azad et al., 2004]) has been shown to improve social interaction and increase social behavior (Trezza et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The neuroligin-3 mutation related to autism causes a disruption in tonic eCB signaling within the hippocampus, resulting in an increase in GABA release and a shift in the E/I balance that is the exact opposite of what was produced by PAK1 disruption.
source: More so, a recent report has indicated that the neuroligin-3 mutation related to autism causes a disruption in tonic eCB signaling within the hippocampus (Földy et al., 2013), resulting in an increase in GABA release and a shift in the E/I balance of the hippocampus that is the exact opposite of what was produced by PAK1 disruption.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: PAK1 disruption has been shown to normalize behavioral changes in the Fragile X model of autism.
source: Finally, PAK1 disruption has also been shown to normalize behavioral changes in the Fragile X model of autism (Dolan et al., 2013; Hayashi et al., 2007), which parallels recent behavioral work similarly demonstrating that administration of AEA, but not 2-AG, hydrolysis inhibitors, can normalize some of the same behavioral deficits seen in Fragile X mice (Qin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Administration of AEA, but not 2-AG, hydrolysis inhibitors can normalize some behavioral deficits seen in Fragile X mice.
source: Finally, PAK1 disruption has also been shown to normalize behavioral changes in the Fragile X model of autism (Dolan et al., 2013; Hayashi et al., 2007), which parallels recent behavioral work similarly demonstrating that administration of AEA, but not 2-AG, hydrolysis inhibitors, can normalize some of the same behavioral deficits seen in Fragile X mice (Qin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Impairments in tonic AEA signaling may relate to the pathology of neurodevelopmental disorders, such as autism.
source: Taken together, while speculative at this time, these data collectively create a compelling picture that impairments in tonic AEA signaling may relate to the pathology of neurodevelopmental disorders, such as autism, and that inhibition of PAK1 may exert its potentially beneficial effects by enhancing tonic AEA signaling.
evidence: This is stated as speculation based on the collective evidence from this and previous studies.

claim: Inhibition of PAK1 may exert its potentially beneficial effects by enhancing tonic AEA signaling.
source: Taken together, while speculative at this time, these data collectively create a compelling picture that impairments in tonic AEA signaling may relate to the pathology of neurodevelopmental disorders, such as autism, and that inhibition of PAK1 may exert its potentially beneficial effects by enhancing tonic AEA signaling.
evidence: This is stated as speculation based on the collective evidence from this and previous studies.

claim: PAK1 has been associated with other disease states including Huntington's disease and Alzheimer's disease.
source: More so, as PAK1 has been associated with other disease states (Gilman et al., 2011; Kelly and Chernoff, 2012; Kumar et al., 2006; Ma et al., 2012), the relationship between PAK1, COX-2 and AEA signaling could prove to be highly relevant for a wide array of pathological processes, given that COX-2 and AEA have similarly been implicated in the etiology of these disease processes (Hermanson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: The relationship between PAK1, COX-2 and AEA signaling could prove to be highly relevant for a wide array of pathological processes.
source: More so, as PAK1 has been associated with other disease states (Gilman et al., 2011; Kelly and Chernoff, 2012; Kumar et al., 2006; Ma et al., 2012), the relationship between PAK1, COX-2 and AEA signaling could prove to be highly relevant for a wide array of pathological processes, given that COX-2 and AEA have similarly been implicated in the etiology of these disease processes (Hermanson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as speculation supported by citations.

claim: COX-2 and AEA have been implicated in the etiology of various disease processes.
source: More so, as PAK1 has been associated with other disease states (Gilman et al., 2011; Kelly and Chernoff, 2012; Kumar et al., 2006; Ma et al., 2012), the relationship between PAK1, COX-2 and AEA signaling could prove to be highly relevant for a wide array of pathological processes, given that COX-2 and AEA have similarly been implicated in the etiology of these disease processes (Hermanson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the literature.

claim: Genetic or pharmacological disruption of PAK1 signaling reduces synaptic COX-2 levels and increases tonic AEA signaling to reduce constitutive GABAergic synaptic transmission in the hippocampus.
source: Specifically, genetic or pharmacological disruption of PAK1 signaling reduces synaptic COX-2 levels and increases tonic AEA signaling to reduce constitutive GABAergic synaptic transmission in the hippocampus.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The effect of PAK1 disruption on GABA transmission is replicated by the direct application of a COX-2 inhibitor, which is also dependent on the activation of presynaptic CB1 receptors.
source: Importantly, this effect of PAK1 disruption on GABA transmission is replicated by the direct application of a COX-2 inhibitor, which is also dependent on the activation of presynaptic CB1 receptors.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 8a,b showing that COX-2 inhibitor mimics PAK1 deletion effects.

claim: In wild type neurons, constitutively active PAK1 is required for maintaining a sufficient level of synaptic COX-2 to keep AEA low, thus less suppression of GABA release and normal inhibitory transmission.
source: In wild type neurons, constitutively active PAK1 is required for maintaining a sufficient level of synaptic COX-2 to keep AEA low, thus less suppression of GABA release and normal inhibitory transmission.
evidence: This is shown in the model diagram in Figure 10 and summarizes the findings.

claim: In the absence of PAK1, synaptic COX-2 is reduced, which leads to accumulation of AEA, increased suppression of GABA release and impaired inhibitory transmission and E/I balance.
source: In the absence of PAK1, synaptic COX-2 is reduced, which leads to accumulation of AEA, increased suppression of GABA release and impaired inhibitory transmission and E/I balance.
evidence: This is shown in the model diagram in Figure 10 and summarizes the findings.
